titre: The Gamble Pasteur Dreaded to Take
accroche: On July 6, 1885, Louis Pasteur tests on a child a treatment he had never dared try on a human being
contenu_vulgarise:
On the morning of July 6, 1885, a nine-year-old boy from Alsace, Joseph Meister, arrives at Louis Pasteur's laboratory in Paris. Two days earlier, a rabid dog bit him fourteen times. Without treatment, rabies is fatal in nearly all cases once symptoms have appeared, and at this date there is no human treatment against it.

## A Protocol Developed on Animals, Never on Humans

Since 1880, Pasteur has been working on rabies with his collaborator Émile Roux. They have developed an attenuation method: fragments of spinal cord from rabid rabbits, hung to dry in open air, gradually lose their virulence until it disappears after two weeks. By inoculating a dog with fragments of increasing virulence, from the most attenuated to the most virulent, Pasteur manages to make it refractory to rabies. The method works reliably on dozens of dogs. But Pasteur, who is not a physician, dreads testing it on a human being.

Faced with Joseph Meister, whose death seems otherwise certain, Pasteur gives in. He does not give the injections himself, he has no right to, and entrusts them to Dr. Jacques-Joseph Grancher. From July 6 to 16, 1885, the child receives thirteen inoculations of spinal cord from rabid rabbits, each a little more virulent than the last. Joseph Meister never develops rabies.

## A Second Trial, Made Public

Pasteur at first keeps silent about this first success, obtained in an emergency and without the methodological safeguards he would have wished for. In September 1885, a second case presents itself: Jean-Baptiste Jupille, a fifteen-year-old shepherd bitten while protecting other shepherds from a rabid dog. The treatment works again. This time, Pasteur makes the matter public and presents his results to the Academy of Sciences.

## The Shift

The news spreads around the world: people who have been bitten flock to Paris from every country to receive the treatment, so numerous that Pasteur has to organize a dedicated vaccination service, which will become the Institut Pasteur in 1888. What this episode reveals goes beyond rabies itself: Pasteur had developed a rigorous protocol on animals, but the move to humans remained, in his own eyes, a gamble without guarantee; the strongest experimental proof never entirely removes the uncertainty of the first trial on a human being, it only makes it defensible.

repere.texte: From July 6 to 16, 1885, Joseph Meister receives thirteen inoculations of spinal cord from rabid rabbits, of increasing virulence. He never develops rabies, the first successful antirabies vaccination in a human being.

carte.punch: Pasteur dreaded testing his treatment on a human; a child left him no choice.
carte.idee: On July 6, 1885, Louis Pasteur tests for the first time on a human a rabies treatment developed on dogs. Thirteen injections save Joseph Meister, bitten fourteen times. This success will lead to the creation of the Institut Pasteur in 1888.

quiz.question: Why does Pasteur hesitate so much before treating Joseph Meister, when his method already worked on dogs?
choix: Because the French government had forbidden any human trial before 1885
Because Joseph Meister had at first refused the treatment
Because he was not a physician and dreaded the consequences of a failure on a human being
Because he doubted that the virus could be transmitted from rabbit to human
quiz.explication: Pasteur is not a physician and has no right to give the injection himself: he dreads, in the absence of any prior human trial, the consequences of a failure on a child, and entrusts the act to Dr. Grancher. No government ban, no doubt about cross-species transmission, and no refusal by Joseph Meister explains this hesitation.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do Pasteur and Émile Roux develop their method of attenuating the rabies virus?
choix: By heating fragments of rabbit spinal cord at high temperature
By letting fragments of spinal cord from rabid rabbits dry, losing their virulence in two weeks
By diluting the virus in a sterile saline solution until it becomes undetectable
By exposing fragments of spinal cord to ultraviolet light for several days
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Fragments of spinal cord from rabid rabbits, hung to dry in open air, gradually lose their virulence until it disappears after two weeks.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who actually gives the injections to Joseph Meister, between July 6 and 16, 1885?
choix: Pasteur himself, despite his lack of medical training
Dr. Jacques-Joseph Grancher, to whom Pasteur entrusts the act
A military nurse requisitioned for the occasion
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pasteur has no right to give the injections himself, not being a physician; he entrusts them to Dr. Jacques-Joseph Grancher.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens in September 1885, with Jean-Baptiste Jupille?
choix: The treatment works again, and Pasteur makes the matter public before the Academy of Sciences
Pasteur refuses to treat him, judging the protocol still too uncertain
The treatment fails for the first time, revealing the limits of the method
Jupille becomes Pasteur's first laboratory assistant at the Institut Pasteur
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The treatment works again on this fifteen-year-old shepherd, bitten while protecting other shepherds, and Pasteur this time presents his results to the Academy of Sciences.
